# The Masonry Modeler

> Masonry estimating software that renders every block — corners, lintels, bond beams, halves, cuts — as you draw. Built by a mason because existing tools count masonry walls like carpet (length × height × factor) instead of modeling them as bonded units. Currently in pre-launch; founder pricing is $300 per seat, per month for the first 10 companies, and that rate is locked for life. Every wall type is included as it comes online — block today, brick, stone and thin brick as they ship, with no upcharge.

## Background

The Masonry Modeler (TMM) is built by Ryan Shanley of Powder River Masonry. The thesis: a masonry wall is not a rectangular field of units to be divided and multiplied. It is a bonded assembly where corners interlock, bond beams wrap, lintels land on specific courses, and non-modular heights produce half-high courses that need their own SKU. Every existing tool treats masonry as a rectangle-counting problem. TMM models the bond first and counts the bond's consequences.

## Core technical rules the engine enforces

- Corners interlock by default; the bond runs through them, inside and outside
- Non-modular leftover is absorbed into the corner — the leg moves 8 inches every course, same as the bond
- Control joints default to 24 feet 8 inches (296 inches = 18.5 blocks × 16 inches exactly); never auto-placed within 16 inches of a corner
- Bond beam courses are driven by the rebar schedule from the structural drawings, not by a checkbox
- Half-high courses are generated and broken out as their own line item, not buried in a waste factor
- The engine will never produce a cut under 4 inches — leftover gets absorbed into adjacent joints or the cut shifts to the next valid position
- 10-inch and 12-inch CMU corners are listed as an 8-inch block plus a face shell spacer (separate line items, the way the supplier ships them)
- Every block-by-block decision is overridable by the mason — one click changes the unit, takeoff updates immediately
- Shop drawings are a byproduct of the model: one trace produces coursed, tagged elevations (numbered courses, grout lifts, openings, finishes, control joints) plus a rebar/dowel layout and a steel bar list — every bar counted by mark and cut length with corner-bend and peak-bend shape codes, not linear feet with a waste factor

## Video proof

A three-minute screen recording of the 88th Avenue pump station being traced and taken off in The Masonry Modeler is embedded on the homepage, the CMU Block Count page, and the Masonry Takeoff Accuracy page. Hosted on YouTube: https://youtu.be/m-fSK2uB924

## Pages

### Architectural (product / topic pages)
- [Home](https://themasonrymodeler.com/): Product overview, hero render of the 88th Avenue pump station, founder waitlist
- [CMU Block Count](https://themasonrymodeler.com/cmu-block-count/): Why block-by-block counting beats square-footage estimating with a factor
- [Bond Beam Estimating](https://themasonrymodeler.com/bond-beam-estimating/): Rebar-driven bond beam scheduling with continuous corner wraps and rebar weight in pounds
- [Masonry Takeoff Accuracy](https://themasonrymodeler.com/masonry-takeoff-accuracy/): The three repeating sources of takeoff error — lintels, corners, half-block courses — and how to eliminate them
- [Masonry Shop Drawings](https://themasonrymodeler.com/masonry-shop-drawings/): Submittal-ready coursed, tagged elevations rendered as you build — openings, special shapes, finishes, bond beams, control joints — plus a rebar/dowel layout and a steel bar list (285 bars, 2,031.4 LF on the sample 15th pod set) counted by mark and cut length. Downloadable 9-sheet sample set.

### Field Notes (blog)
- [Blog Index](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/)
- [Why I Built The Masonry Modeler](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/why-i-built-this/): Founder story — the Douglas Humane Society job where the rectangle-counter model became impossible to ignore
- [The Software Sees the Corner. Why Am I Placing It?](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/software-sees-the-corner/): On automatic corner detection, the cost premium of corner SKUs, and the half-high-course miss
- [The Corner Test](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/the-corner-test/): A one-minute test for any masonry estimating tool — whether it was built from the coursing or from areas. A tool that fails it cannot be patched
- [Half the Block, Two-Thirds the Price](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/half-block-cost/): A half block costs roughly two-thirds of a full unit. Halves fall out of the coursing, so area math can never produce a half count
- [Stop Guessing Your Half Block Order](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/stop-guessing-half-block-order/): Why the 20% rule breaks down once a job mixes bullnose, split-face, colors and multiple widths — "halves" stopped being one line item
- [What a Masonry Shop Drawing Submittal Must Show](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/whats-on-a-masonry-shop-drawing/): The required contents of a masonry submittal — coursing, special shapes, reinforcing, control joints, opening dimensions
- [Masonry Shop Drawings in SketchUp — and Why You Shouldn't](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/masonry-shop-drawings-in-sketchup/): SketchUp draws boxes and has no concept of coursing, bond or special units, so every unit tag is hand work
- [We All Label Shop Drawings in Bluebeam by Hand. Why?](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/bluebeam-shop-drawings/): The common workflow — export the render, mark it up in Bluebeam, label every opening and course by hand — and why the drawing should label itself
- [What Skipping the Shop Drawing Costs You](https://themasonrymodeler.com/blog/what-skipping-the-shop-drawing-costs/): The case for a set on every job even when nobody requires one. On one project the per-sheet piece tables totalled 12,624 units against an order of 11,485 — the 1,139 difference was corner units appearing on two elevations, roughly nine percent of the order riding on one line of reconciliation

## About the founder

Ryan Shanley is the founder of Powder River Masonry and the builder of The Masonry Modeler. He does masonry takeoffs by hand in spreadsheets because the available estimating tools do not model masonry. TMM is the tool he wanted and could not find.
